title: Lakshmana's line
hook: a line in the dust, a holy man at the door, and a sacred duty turned into a trap
carry: maryada: the guest is god, the line holds
tomorrow: the holy man is Ravana. who tries to stop him?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cry, a dying demon in Rama's voice, and Lakshmana driven from the hut. Viveka: telling the real from the fake. Now Sita is alone. Almost.
screen: `VIVEKA: TELLING THE REAL FROM THE FAKE.`

segments.voice: Before Lakshmana leaves, in a later telling of the story, he does one last thing. With an arrow, he draws a line in the dust all the way around the hut. Stay inside this line, he tells Sita, whatever happens, whoever comes. Nothing evil can cross it. Then he runs into the forest. The clearing goes quiet. A few minutes later, a holy man walks out of the trees: an old wandering ascetic with a staff and a begging bowl, chanting softly. He stops at the edge of the line. And, very politely, he asks for food.
screen: `A LINE IN THE DUST.` → `STAY INSIDE IT.` → `A HOLY MAN AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The holy man is Ravana in disguise. In that telling, he can't cross the line, so he needs Sita to cross it. He asks for alms. She offers them from inside. He says: a holy man can't take food from someone behind a barrier. Come out and give it properly, or I'll leave, and you'll have turned away a guest. That's the trap, and it's built from a real Hindu teaching: atithi devo bhava, treat the guest as God. Feeding whoever comes to the door is a sacred duty, and Sita was raised on it. So she lifts her foot and steps over. One thing, plainly: the line isn't in Valmiki's Ramayana. In Valmiki, Lakshmana just leaves, and Sita welcomes the disguised Ravana as a guest, with water and food. The line grew in later retellings, and it became a phrase: a Lakshmana rekha is a limit you must not cross. Hindus have an older word for that kind of limit: maryada, the boundary of right conduct. It's why Rama is called Maryada Purushottam, the best of men, who keeps every limit. The story holds both teachings at once. The guest is God; Hindu homes still feed whoever comes. And a sacred duty can be borrowed by someone who means harm. Ravana didn't break Sita's goodness. He used it. Maryada is the line that keeps your kindness your own. In a family, at a job, with a friend who knows exactly which kind word will make you bend, it's the same question: is this generosity, or is someone using it?
screen: `RAVANA NEEDS HER TO CROSS.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.` · `NOT IN VALMIKI. IT GREW LATER.` · `MARYADA: THE LIMIT OF RIGHT CONDUCT.` · then, large: `THE GUEST IS GOD. THE LINE HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes still cook a little extra for whoever might come to the door. Picture your own door, and someone you'd feed gladly. Then picture your line: one thing you won't do, even for someone polite, even when crossing would look kind. Say it once, quietly, the way Lakshmana drew his in the dust.
Lakshmana rekha. Lakshmana's line: drawn around the hut in later tellings, and now an everyday phrase for a limit you must not cross.
Take this with you: maryada. The guest is God, and the line holds. Day fifty-one, done.

screen: `DAY 51 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO TRIES TO STOP RAVANA?`

howItsDone: In everyday speech across India, a Lakshmana rekha is a boundary that must not be crossed, and Rama is called Maryada Purushottam, the one who keeps every limit; many Hindu homes still treat the guest as God, and the line around the hut is a well-known Ramlila moment though it is not in Valmiki.

The Lakshmana rekha is absent from Valmiki. Its earliest attestation is uncertain; it is often linked to later regional retellings, and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas has Mandodari allude to Lakshmana's line in the Lanka Kanda. Keeper/scholar to confirm and, if desired, name the source.
'Treat the guest as God' (atithi devo bhava) is from Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2; paraphrased. Confirm.
Ravana's argument (can't take alms across a barrier) follows popular tellings; confirm.
